advancement.title: Advancement
advancement.summary: A level is a budget of points, spent in the same shop as character creation — discipline grades, skill ranks, or mastery hit points.
advancement.summary_html: A level is a budget of points, spent in the same shop as character creation — discipline grades, skill ranks, or mastery hit points.
advancement.html:
A level in Ico is not a template. It is a budget of 15 points and a clock that raises your skill ceilings, and it is spent in exactly the same shop as Creating a Character — there is nothing you can buy on levelling that you could not have bought at the start, and nothing you bought at the start that is now closed to you.

What a level gives

  • 15 points to spend, as below.
  • 3 mastery hit points, free

and automatic. Everyone gets these; they are the baseline survival curve that used to come from a class.

  • 1 power, chosen from a pool you have

opened — see Disciplines and Discipline Powers.

  • Every 4 levels, one

attribute point.

  • One more rank of headroom on every skill ceiling, per Using and Focusing Skills.

What points buy

  • A discipline grade — at the cost listed in Disciplines.
  • One rank in a skill — at the cost listed in Using and Focusing Skills, which

depends on how that skill is focused.

  • Mastery hit points — one point buys

2 of them, but no more than 1 bought per level may be added on top of the free grant. Without that ceiling a character with nothing else to buy turns every spare point into padding, and fights get longer every level rather than deadlier.

  • Stamina or spirit — one point buys

3 points of one power source, to a limit of 3 points spent per level. Powers get more expensive as you reach further with them, so a character who never widens the reservoir slowly loses access to their own best tricks.

Both ceilings are per level and cumulative: a character who skipped them last level may catch up on this one. What they prevent is a character with nothing left to buy converting an entire level into one runaway statistic.

Mastery hit points are cheap per point precisely because a skill rank keeps paying out on every roll you ever make and a mastery hit point absorbs its damage once. Both are worth buying; neither should be obviously correct.

The per-level mastery grant is deliberately small next to the opening reserve in Creating a Character. Hit points that climb steeply every level while damage stays flat do not make a character heroic, they make every fight longer than the last; the curve here is meant to be nearly flat, with the growth in what a character can do rather than in how long they take to kill.

Core hit points are not on this list. They remain equal to your constitution and grow only when that attribute does — see Core and Mastery Hit Points. A character's real durability stays almost flat for life, and everything the levels add is the cushion in front of it.

armour.title: Armour and Shields
armour.summary: Armour points reduce every blow that lands, at the price of a skill penalty that also makes a dodging wearer easier to hit. Shields add to a block instead.
armour.summary_html: Armour points reduce every blow that lands, at the price of a skill penalty that also makes a dodging wearer easier to hit. Shields add to a block instead.
armour.html:
Armour is worn for its armour points (AP), subtracted from every blow that lands — see Working Out Damage. The price is a skill penalty that applies while it is worn and, because a dodging defender's targeting difficulty is built from their dodge skill, makes the wearer easier to hit when dodging. See Landing a Blow, and the Untouchable signature in Discipline Powers, which removes exactly that penalty.

Light armour

  • Partial leather — AP 1, skill

penalty 0, 5gp.

  • Leather — AP 2, skill penalty

-1, 10gp.

  • Studded leather — AP 3, skill

penalty -2, 25gp.

  • Chain shirt — AP 4, skill penalty

-3, 100gp.

Medium and heavy armour

  • Scale mail — AP 4, skill penalty

-4, 50gp.

  • Chain mail — AP 5, skill penalty

-4, 150gp.

  • Breastplate — AP 5, skill penalty

-3, 200gp.

  • Full plate — AP 8, skill penalty

-6, 1500gp.

Shields

A shield does nothing while you dodge. While you block, it adds to your targeting difficulty and its armour points come off the blow on top of your worn armour.

  • Buckler — block bonus +1,

block AP 2, 5gp.

  • Shield — block bonus +2,

block AP 3, 15gp.

  • Great shield — block bonus

+3, block AP 5, skill penalty -1, 40gp.

attributes.title: Attributes
attributes.summary: Every character has six attributes — three physical, three mental — that describe their raw potential.
attributes.summary_html: Every character has six attributes — three physical, three mental — that describe their raw potential.
attributes.html:
A character's core potential is captured by 6 attributes. The physical ones are strength, dexterity and constitution; the mental ones are intelligence, willpower and charisma.

Reading a score

A score of 10 is average for a capable adult. Every 2 points above 10 gives a +1 bonus that applies to rolls governed by that attribute; every 2 points below gives a matching -1 penalty. A character's race can modify the raw scores before this bonus is worked out.

Which attribute governs which action is set by the skill in use — see Using and Focusing Skills — and attribute bonuses are one of the inputs to the core roll.

character-creation.title: Creating a Character
character-creation.summary: Spend a fixed pool of attribute points, choose skill focus, trade mastery hit points against skill points, take one power, and start with a set purse.
character-creation.summary_html: Spend a fixed pool of attribute points, choose skill focus, trade mastery hit points against skill points, take one power, and start with a set purse.
character-creation.html:
Build a starting character in this order.

Attributes

Split 80 points among the six Attributes. No score may start below 3 or above 18. Race modifiers apply after this spread, and the bonus for a high score is worked out from the final number.

Disciplines

Spend a budget of 20 points on Disciplines. That is enough for Adept in one, or Initiate in several — the first is a specialist, the second a generalist, and both are legitimate opening positions. The grades you buy set which skill groups are focused, unfocused and peripheral, per Using and Focusing Skills.

Mastery hit points and skill points

You have 30 points for skill ranks and mastery hit points together, spent at the same prices Advancement uses at every later level — there is no special chargen exchange rate. You may start with at most 25 mastery hit points however much you are willing to spend.

That ceiling is deliberately generous compared with what a level adds later. A starting character has almost no cushion in front of their core hit points, and without a real opening reserve first-level fights end in two exchanges.

Powers and money

Take 1 power (see Using a Power) and 150 gold pieces to equip yourself from Weapons and Armour and Shields.

Priorities

Finally, apply your Setting Priorities — the trades that let one character start stronger in an area at the cost of being weaker, or more encumbered by circumstance, elsewhere.

core-resolution.title: The Core Roll
core-resolution.summary: Most actions are a d20 plus bonuses against either a fixed difficulty or an opposed roll. Beating the target by more means a better result.
core-resolution.summary_html: Most actions are a d20 plus bonuses against either a fixed difficulty or an opposed roll. Beating the target by more means a better result.
core-resolution.html:
When the outcome of an action is in doubt, you roll for it, and it is almost always the same roll.

The roll

Roll 1d20 and add your bonuses — from attributes, from the relevant skill, and from environmental factors the Dungeon Master calls out. Compare the total to a target, which is either:

  • a fixed difficulty set by the Dungeon Master, or
  • an opposed roll: someone else's 1d20

plus their own bonuses.

Meet or beat the target and you succeed — a total exactly equal to the target is a success, everywhere in the game. Combat is not an exception: a blow that matches the targeting difficulty lands, just as a power that matches its difficulty works.

Margin matters

Beating the target by more points is a better outcome, not just a success: more damage on a blow, less effort spent on a power, a faster or cleaner result. Individual rules say how their own margin is spent — see Landing a Blow and Working Out Damage for the combat case, and Using a Power for powers.

damage.title: Working Out Damage
damage.summary: Damage is the weapon's rating plus half the amount the attack beat the targeting difficulty, then reduced by armour and any block.
damage.summary_html: Damage is the weapon's rating plus half the amount the attack beat the targeting difficulty, then reduced by armour and any block.
damage.html:
Damage is only worked out once a blow has landed — see Landing a Blow.

The raw figure

Take the weapon's damage rating and add 0.5 times the amount by which the attack roll beat the targeting difficulty, rounding down. A weapon that beats a defence cleanly therefore does noticeably more than one that scrapes past it.

Skill in the blow

Add one further point of damage for every 8 full ranks of the attack skill you used, counting the bonus from its governing attribute.

This is the term that keeps the game moving. Attack and defence rise together as characters advance, so the margin on a typical hit does not grow — without a term tied directly to skill, a veteran's blows would land exactly as hard as a novice's while everyone's mastery hit points climbed every level, and every fight would take longer than the last one. A more practised fighter does not merely connect more often; they land blows that matter.

Reductions

The raw figure is then reduced:

  • by the armour rating of whatever the target is wearing, applied to

every blow — see Armour and Shields;

  • and, if the defender was blocking, by the armour points of the weapon

or shield used to block.

The half a blow that always lands

Armour and a raised shield together may never take more than 0.5 of a blow's raw damage. However heavy the plate and however broad the shield, at least half of what got through the defence gets through the armour too.

Without this floor the arithmetic breaks at the top end: plate and a great shield subtract more than a sword's entire damage rating, so the best-armoured character in the party stops being hard to kill and becomes impossible to kill, and every light weapon in Weapons turns into a prop. The cap keeps heavy armour excellent without letting it leave the game.

Applying it

Whatever is left comes off the target's hit points, taking mastery hit points first and reaching core hit points only once mastery is gone.

discipline-list.title: The Five Disciplines
discipline-list.summary: Martial, Athletic, Awareness, Magical and Spiritual — each with a skill group, a power pool, and one signature ability at Master grade.
discipline-list.summary_html: Martial, Athletic, Awareness, Magical and Spiritual — each with a skill group, a power pool, and one signature ability at Master grade.
discipline-list.html:
Each discipline names a group of skills from the The Skill List, draws its powers from one of the two Stamina and Spirit, and grants a single signature ability at Master grade. Grades and costs are in Disciplines.

Martial

Skill group: melee attack, ranged attack, block, fortitude. Source: stamina.

Weapon work, and the endurance to keep doing it. Its powers hit harder and find the weak points in armour.

Signature — Killing Blow. You convert the margin by which your attack beat the targeting difficulty into damage at full value instead of half. See Working Out Damage for the ordinary conversion.

Athletic

Skill group: dodge, climb, jump, balance, swim, escape artist, move silently. Source: stamina.

Speed and body control. Its powers add attacks, add movement, and make you harder to pin down.

Signature — Untouchable. Armour's skill penalty no longer worsens your targeting difficulty when you dodge.

Awareness

Skill group: spot, listen, search, sense motive, appraise, disable device. Source: stamina.

Noticing things in time to act on them.

Signature — Read the Blow. You may choose whether to dodge or block after seeing the attack roll, rather than before. See Landing a Blow.

Magical

Skill group: spellcasting, concentration, knowledge (arcana), decipher script, use magic device. Source: spirit.

Constructed magic, learned from books and study. See How Spellcasting Works.

Signature — School Mastery. Choose one school of magic. Spells of that school are cast at reduced difficulty.

Spiritual

Skill group: willpower, heal, diplomacy, knowledge (religion). Source: spirit.

Granted magic, and the strength of will that carries it.

Signature — Granted Domain. Choose one domain of influence. Spells of that domain are cast at heavily reduced difficulty — this is what a god being your power source is worth. The size of both reductions is given in Discipline Powers.

discipline-powers.title: Discipline Powers
discipline-powers.summary: The powers each discipline opens, and the signature ability each grants at Master grade. Every power scales — you choose how hard to push it.
discipline-powers.summary_html: The powers each discipline opens, and the signature ability each grants at Master grade. Every power scales — you choose how hard to push it.
discipline-powers.html:
These powers are opened by holding the matching discipline at the matching grade — see Disciplines. The General Powers stay open to everyone regardless. All of them are used as Using a Power describes: you declare a difficulty, roll, and pay for what you asked for.

Martial

Power Attack (Initiate; stamina, melee attack, base difficulty 4) — a heavier swing at the cost of control. Each further 2 points of difficulty adds 1 damage to the blow.

Find the Gap (Adept; stamina, melee attack, base difficulty 6) — a blow aimed at a join or a strap. Each further 2 points of difficulty ignores 1 point of the target's damage reduction -- worn armour and a raised shield alike, since the whole point is that you are not hitting either of them. This is the answer to heavy armour, and it is deliberately a power rather than a weapon property.

Killing Blow (Master signature) — your attacks convert margin into damage at 1 per point instead of the usual half. See Working Out Damage.

Athletic

Redouble (Initiate; stamina, dodge, base difficulty 4) — thrown weight and a second movement. Each further 10 points of difficulty adds 1 to your targeting difficulty against one attack, if you are dodging.

The price per point looks steep next to Power Attack, and it is: a point of targeting difficulty applies to every attack aimed at you for as long as you can pay for it, while a point of damage is spent once. Priced to match Power Attack point for point, this power made a practised dodger effectively unhittable.

Sneak Attack (Adept; stamina, melee attack, base difficulty 6) — usable only against a target who is unaware of you or already engaged with someone else. Each further 2 points of difficulty adds 2 damage.

Untouchable (Master signature) — armour's skill penalty no longer worsens your targeting difficulty while dodging, so you may wear real protection without surrendering your defence. See Armour and Shields.

Awareness

Forewarned (Initiate; stamina, spot, base difficulty 4) — you saw it coming. Each further 2 points of difficulty adds 2 to your place in the order for the coming fight.

Read the Blow (Master signature) — you may choose whether to dodge or block after the attack roll has been made rather than before, inverting the usual guess in Landing a Blow.

Magical and Spiritual

Both of these disciplines take their powers from the spell lists rather than from a separate pool — a spell is a power, as How Spellcasting Works explains. What their grades buy is reach: an Initiate may hold and cast spells at all, and an Adept's focused spellcasting skill lets them carry a much higher difficulty.

School Mastery (Magical, Master signature) — choose one school of magic. Spells of that school are cast at 5 less difficulty.

Granted Domain (Spiritual, Master signature) — choose one domain of influence. Spells of that domain are cast at 10 less difficulty. This is the mechanical weight of having a god as your power source, and it is larger than School Mastery because it is narrower: a domain is a subject, a school is a technique.

disciplines.title: Disciplines
disciplines.summary: Disciplines replace classes. Each is bought in three named grades, and the grade you hold sets your focus in that discipline's skill group and opens its power pool.
disciplines.summary_html: Disciplines replace classes. Each is bought in three named grades, and the grade you hold sets your focus in that discipline's skill group and opens its power pool.
disciplines.html:
Ico has no classes. What a character is good at comes from the disciplines they have taken, and a character may hold as many as they can afford.

Grades

Every discipline is bought in three grades — Initiate, Adept, then Master — in that order, paid for with advancement points (see Advancement):

  • Initiate costs 5 points.
  • Adept costs a further 15 points.
  • Master costs a further 40 points.

The cost curve is the only limit on how many disciplines you hold. Going wide is cheap and going deep is expensive, deliberately.

What a grade does

A grade does exactly three things, and nothing else:

  • It sets your focus in that discipline's skill group. A discipline

you hold at Initiate makes its group unfocused; at Adept or Master it makes the group focused. Any group you hold no discipline in stays peripheral. Focus governs how far a skill can be raised and what each rank costs — see Using and Focusing Skills.

  • It opens that discipline's power pool at the matching grade, so

you may take its powers when you gain one. See Discipline Powers.

  • At Master only, it grants that discipline's single signature

ability.

Because focus is derived from grade, there is no separate multiclassing rule and nothing to reconcile when a character advances in two directions at once. The five disciplines and their signatures are listed in the The Five Disciplines.

The familiar archetypes

Nothing stops you building the classic adventuring roles — they are combinations rather than categories. A fighter is Martial and Athletic; a rogue is Athletic and Awareness; a wizard is Magical and Awareness; a priest is Spiritual with a little Martial. A character who spreads Initiate grades across four disciplines is a generalist, and that is a legitimate build rather than a mistake.

general-powers.title: General Powers
general-powers.summary: Powers open to every character regardless of discipline. Like all powers they scale: you choose how far to push the difficulty.
general-powers.summary_html: Powers open to every character regardless of discipline. Like all powers they scale: you choose how far to push the difficulty.
general-powers.html:
These powers are open to any character, whatever Disciplines they hold. Each is written with its power source, its skill, and its base difficulty; all are resolved as Using a Power describes.

Fast Attack

(stamina, the attack skill in use, base difficulty 1; each further 15 points of difficulty grants one more extra attack)

Attack again, after your first. Declare how many extra attacks you are going for, roll once, and use that single roll for two things: first against the declared difficulty to see whether the power worked and what it cost, then against the target's targeting difficulty for each attack it granted.

Melee and ranged both use this one power, taking whichever attack skill the weapon calls for. It replaces the separate Fast Melee and Fast Ranged powers of earlier drafts, which were the same power written three times.

Second Wind

(stamina, fortitude, base difficulty 8; each further 3 points of difficulty recovers 2 more)

Shrug off a near miss and keep going, recovering mastery hit points but never core hit points. Real wounds do not respond to willpower.

hit-points.title: Core and Mastery Hit Points
hit-points.summary: Core hit points are your body and equal your constitution. Mastery hit points are luck and skill, and soak harm first.
hit-points.summary_html: Core hit points are your body and equal your constitution. Mastery hit points are luck and skill, and soak harm first.
hit-points.html:
Characters have two separate pools of hit points, and they mean different things.

Core hit points

Core hit points (CHP) are physical hardiness and the sheer will to keep going. A character's core hit points equal their constitution. Losing core hit points means real damage — a wound that actually landed.

Mastery hit points

Mastery hit points (MHP) are an accumulated cushion of luck, skill and experience. Losing mastery hit points is a near miss, a blow softened by rolling with it, a fight-ending strike that turned out to graze. They are bought as a character is built and advanced, traded against skill points — see Creating a Character.

Which pool takes the hit

Harm comes off mastery hit points first, and only reaches core hit points once mastery is exhausted. Working Out Damage covers how the size of a hit is worked out before it is applied here.

hitting.title: Landing a Blow
hitting.summary: The defender dodges or blocks, which sets the targeting difficulty. The attacker rolls d20 plus attack skill and must match or beat it.
hitting.summary_html: The defender dodges or blocks, which sets the targeting difficulty. The attacker rolls d20 plus attack skill and must match or beat it.
hitting.html:
Every blow is one attacker against one defender.

The defender chooses

Before the attack is rolled, the defender chooses to dodge or block, and that choice sets the targeting difficulty (TD) the attacker must beat.

  • Against a dodging defender, the TD is

10 plus the defender's dodge skill, before other modifiers. Most armour carries a dodge penalty, which lowers this number and makes a dodging wearer easier to hit.

  • Against a blocking defender, the TD is the defender's block skill,

usually modified by the block bonus or penalty of the weapon or shield being used.

The attacker rolls

The attacker rolls 1d20 plus their attack skill and applicable modifiers — see The Core Roll, and Using and Focusing Skills for which attack skill applies to which weapon. If the total matches or beats the targeting difficulty, the blow lands and Working Out Damage is worked out. A total exactly equal to the TD is a hit that carries no margin: it lands for the weapon's damage and nothing more.

The amount by which the roll exceeded the TD is carried into the damage step, so a cleaner hit hurts more. Combat uses the same threshold as every other roll in the game — see the core roll — rather than a stricter one of its own.

Weapon and shield block values used above are listed with the Weapons and Armour and Shields.

power-sources.title: Stamina and Spirit
power-sources.summary: Physical powers spend stamina, based on constitution. Magical powers spend spirit, based on will.
power-sources.summary_html: Physical powers spend stamina, based on constitution. Magical powers spend spirit, based on will.
power-sources.html:
There are two power sources, and every power draws on one of them.

  • Stamina fuels physical powers. Its base value is a character's

constitution.

  • Spirit fuels magical powers, spells included. Its base value is a

character's will.

Both can be raised by advancement, and possibly by items. Using a Power covers what a power costs from its source and how a good roll reduces that cost.

priorities.title: Setting Priorities
priorities.summary: A pool of priority points buys advantages at character creation, and can be topped up by taking matching disadvantages.
priorities.summary_html: A pool of priority points buys advantages at character creation, and can be topped up by taking matching disadvantages.
priorities.html:
Each character gets a number of priority points set by the Dungeon Master; the standard allowance is 4. Spend them on advantages, and take disadvantages to get more. This is done once, as part of Creating a Character.

Attributes

  • Spend 1 point for 4 extra

attribute points.

  • Gain 1 point by giving up

4 attribute points.

Skills

  • Spend 1 point for 5 extra skill

points, up to the normal skill maxima.

  • Spend 1 point to raise the maximum level of a single skill by one

step; this persists as the character advances.

  • Gain 1 point by giving up 5

skill points.

Powers

  • Spend 1 point for one extra power.
  • Gain 1 point by taking one fewer power.
  • Spend 1 point for a permanent

+3 bonus to one power source. This may only be taken once.

Wealth and circumstance

  • Spend 1 point for 500 extra

starting gold.

  • Spend 1 point for low-level connections;

spend two for high-level connections.

  • Spend two points to begin play landed.
  • Gain 1 point by starting with

100 less gold.

  • Gain 1 point by taking low-level enemies;

gain two by taking high-level enemies.

skill-list.title: The Skill List
skill-list.summary: Every skill and the attribute that governs it. Some governing attributes are not yet assigned.
skill-list.summary_html: Every skill and the attribute that governs it. Some governing attributes are not yet assigned.
skill-list.html:
Each entry is a skill and its governing attribute. Entries marked unassigned are carried over from an earlier draft and still need a governing attribute chosen; treat them as Dungeon-Master's-call for now. How high any of these can be raised depends on its focus tier — see Using and Focusing Skills.

Combat skills

  • Attack (melee) — strength. Used to hit with melee weapons.
  • Attack (ranged) — dexterity. Used to hit with ranged weapons, and

to place spells that need an attack roll.

  • Block — strength. Sets the targeting difficulty when blocking.
  • Dodge — dexterity. Sets the targeting difficulty when

dodging.

  • Fortitude — constitution. Resisting physical duress: poison,

disease, exhaustion.

  • Willpower — willpower. Resisting mental duress: fear, domination,

pain.

Magic

  • Spellcasting — intelligence or willpower. The single skill used to

cast every spell; see How Spellcasting Works.

  • Concentration — constitution.
  • Use magic device — unassigned.

General skills

  • Appraise — intelligence.
  • Balance — dexterity.
  • Bluff — charisma.
  • Climb — strength.
  • Craft — intelligence.
  • Decipher script — intelligence.
  • Diplomacy — charisma.
  • Disable device — intelligence.
  • Disguise — charisma.
  • Escape artist — dexterity.
  • Forgery — intelligence.
  • Gather information — unassigned.
  • Handle animal — unassigned.
  • Heal — unassigned.
  • Hide — unassigned.
  • Intimidate — unassigned.
  • Jump — unassigned.
  • Listen — unassigned.
  • Move silently — unassigned.
  • Open lock — unassigned.
  • Perform — unassigned.
  • Profession — unassigned.
  • Ride — unassigned.
  • Search — unassigned.
  • Sense motive — unassigned.
  • Sleight of hand — unassigned.
  • Speak language — unassigned.
  • Spot — unassigned.
  • Survival — unassigned.
  • Swim — unassigned.
  • Use rope — unassigned.

Knowledge skills

Each is a separate skill, all currently unassigned for governing attribute: arcana; architecture and engineering; dungeoneering; geography; history; local; nature; nobility; religion; the planes.

skills.title: Using and Focusing Skills
skills.summary: A skill check is d20 plus the skill. Focus — set by the disciplines you hold — decides how high a skill can be raised and what each rank costs.
skills.summary_html: A skill check is d20 plus the skill. Focus — set by the disciplines you hold — decides how high a skill can be raised and what each rank costs.
skills.html:
Making a check

A skill check is the core roll: 1d20 plus the skill's rank plus the bonus from its governing attribute, against a fixed difficulty or an opposed roll. Each skill has one governing attribute, listed in the The Skill List.

Focus

Skills are grouped, and each group sits at one of three tiers — focused, unfocused or peripheral — decided entirely by which Disciplines you hold and at what grade. You never choose a focus tier directly.

Focus does two things.

It sets a ceiling. The highest rank a skill can be raised to is 1 per level, on top of a base that depends on focus: 3 for focused skills, 2 for unfocused, and 0 for peripheral. The gaps are narrow on purpose — a specialist should be reliably better, not the only person in the party who can attempt the thing at all.

It sets a price. One rank costs 1 advancement point in a focused skill, 2 in an unfocused one, and 3 in a peripheral one — see Advancement. This is where specialisation is really expressed: a generalist is not forbidden from keeping pace, merely made to spend everything doing it.

spell-list.title: The Spell List
spell-list.summary: The spells defined so far, each with its difficulty, school, domain and other properties.
spell-list.summary_html: The spells defined so far, each with its difficulty, school, domain and other properties.
spell-list.html:
Each spell is written with its base difficulty in brackets, then its properties. Difficulty, cost and boosting all work as How Spellcasting Works and Standard Spell Properties describe.

Cure / Cause Wounds (16)

  • Schools: life force
  • Domains: healing, or harm when reversed
  • Range: touch
  • Minimum spirit: 1

Restores hit point damage to the recipient. Cast as Cause Wounds, the same spell instead inflicts damage.

Force Bolt (2)

  • Schools: energy
  • Domains: magic
  • Range: 10, needs an attack roll
  • Damage: 4 (force)
  • Save: none
  • Minimum spirit: 0

Fires bolts of magical energy that deal force damage. Non-standard boosts:

  • Extra bolts: +4 difficulty per additional bolt.
  • Damage boost: +1 damage per bolt for each +1 difficulty.

spell-properties.title: Standard Spell Properties
spell-properties.summary: Range, duration, area and accuracy work the same across almost all spells, and can usually be boosted by casting at a higher difficulty.
spell-properties.summary_html: Range, duration, area and accuracy work the same across almost all spells, and can usually be boosted by casting at a higher difficulty.
spell-properties.html:
Most spells share these properties. Unless a spell says otherwise, each can be boosted by choosing to cast at a higher difficulty than the minimum — see How Spellcasting Works and Using a Power for what raising the difficulty costs.

Range

A spell's range is self, touch, or a number.

  • Self — the spell only ever affects the caster.
  • Touch — the caster affects themselves or another recipient by

touching them. Touching an unwilling target needs a melee attack roll.

  • A number — a range in grid squares, each square being

2 metres (roughly 2 yards). If the spell needs an attack roll to land, the listed number is short range and long range is 2 times it; use the ranged attack skill to hit. Range can be extended by 1 square per point of added difficulty.

Duration and area of effect

These are defined per spell for now; there is no general rule yet.

Accuracy

A spell's standard accuracy is 0 — no bonus or penalty to the attack roll. Accuracy increases by +1 for every point of added difficulty.

spellcasting.title: How Spellcasting Works
spellcasting.summary: Spells are powers cast with the spellcasting skill, paid for in spirit. Each spell has a school (how it is built) and a domain (what it does).
spellcasting.summary_html: Spells are powers cast with the spellcasting skill, paid for in spirit. Each spell has a school (how it is built) and a domain (what it does).
spellcasting.html:
Spells as powers

Every spell is a power. There is one casting skill — spellcasting — and one power source for all magic: spirit (see Stamina and Spirit). A spell's difficulty is used exactly as any other power's difficulty, and a margin over it reduces the spirit cost the same way.

School and domain

Every spell is tagged with both:

  • a school of magic — how the spell is constructed: life force,

energy, matter, rifts, influence and command, or illusion;

  • a domain of influence — what the spell actually does: healing,

war, trickery, love, death, nature, or magic.

A caster's access to spells, and any bonus when casting them, is described in terms of these schools and domains.

Shared properties

Beyond its own effect, every spell has a standard set of properties — range, duration, area of effect, accuracy — covered in Standard Spell Properties. The The Spell List gives the spells themselves.

using-powers.title: Using a Power
using-powers.summary: Declare how hard you are pushing, roll the power's skill against that difficulty, and pay 10 plus the difficulty minus your roll — never less than a third of the difficulty.
using-powers.summary_html: Declare how hard you are pushing, roll the power's skill against that difficulty, and pay 10 plus the difficulty minus your roll — never less than a third of the difficulty.
using-powers.html:
Declare, then roll

Every power lists a base difficulty, a skill, and a step: how much extra difficulty buys one more increment of effect. Before rolling, you declare the difficulty you are attempting — the base, plus however many steps you want. Then roll that skill as the core roll. Meeting the declared difficulty means the power works, at the scale you asked for.

This is why a power never becomes free with experience. Growing skill does not make the same effect cheaper; it makes a larger effect reachable at the same price. The scaling steps for each power are given in General Powers and Discipline Powers; spells work the same way and call it boosting, in Standard Spell Properties.

The cost

A successful power costs base_cost + difficulty - skill_roll points from its power source, where the base cost is 10 and every point by which the roll beat the difficulty takes 1 off.

No power ever costs less than its declared difficulty divided by 3, rounded down. Reaching further always costs more, however good the roll, and this floor is what keeps stamina and spirit meaningful for a veteran.

One roll, two jobs

When a power is invoked on an action that uses the same skill — a melee attack power rolled on melee attack, say — you make one roll and it serves both purposes: first against the declared difficulty to settle whether the power worked and what it cost, then against the target's targeting difficulty to resolve the action itself. You never roll twice for one swing.

Failure

If the roll misses the declared difficulty, the power does not happen, the action is spent, and you pay the minimum cost anyway. That risk is the reason not to declare the highest difficulty you can imagine every time: pushing further increases the effect, the price, and the chance of getting nothing.

weapons.title: Weapons
weapons.summary: Weapon statistics: accuracy modifier, damage rating, size, and the armour points it contributes when used to block.
weapons.summary_html: Weapon statistics: accuracy modifier, damage rating, size, and the armour points it contributes when used to block.
weapons.html:
Each weapon carries the statistics that feed Landing a Blow and Working Out Damage: an accuracy modifier to the attack roll, a damage rating, a size, and the block value in armour points it subtracts from a blow when you use it to block rather than dodge.

Simple melee weapons

  • Dagger — accuracy +2, damage

4, size S, block 2, 2gp.

  • Short sword — accuracy +1,

damage 6, size S, block 6, 10gp.

  • Hand axe — accuracy +0, damage

7, size S, block 3, 8gp.

  • Staff — accuracy +0, damage

5, size M, block 7, 1gp.

Martial melee weapons

  • Sword — accuracy +1, damage

8, size M, block 5, 20gp.

  • Battle axe — accuracy +0,

damage 9, size M, block 3, 20gp.

  • Two-handed sword — accuracy

+0, damage 12, size L, block 4, 50gp.

  • Great axe — accuracy +0, damage

12, size L, block 2, 45gp.

Finesse

A weapon of size S may use dexterity instead of strength for its attack skill. Without this the game has no nimble fighter in it at all: melee attack is a strength skill while dodge is a dexterity one, so a character built around speed was obliged to be bad at hitting things no matter which weapon they picked, and the whole light-and-quick archetype collapsed into a worse heavy fighter.

Ranged weapons are not yet statted. The larger weapons are two-handed and cannot be combined with a shield from Armour and Shields.

ch-advancement.title: Disciplines and Advancement
ch-advancement.summary: How a character specialises, and how they grow.
ch-advancement.summary_html: How a character specialises, and how they grow.
ch-advancement.html: Ico has no classes. Specialisation is bought in pieces, from a menu that never closes, and a level is simply the next instalment of the budget you spend on that menu.

ch-characters.title: Characters
ch-characters.summary: Attributes, the two pools of hit points, and how a starting character is built.
ch-characters.summary_html: Attributes, the two pools of hit points, and how a starting character is built.
ch-characters.html: A character is six attributes, two pools of hit points, a spread of skills, and a handful of powers. This chapter covers the first two and the process that sets all of them at the start of play.

ch-combat.title: Combat
ch-combat.summary: Landing a blow, and turning a hit into lost hit points.
ch-combat.summary_html: Landing a blow, and turning a hit into lost hit points.
ch-combat.html: Combat resolves one blow at a time. First the attacker tries to hit a defender who is either dodging or blocking; then, if the blow lands, its damage is worked out and applied.

ch-equipment.title: Equipment
ch-equipment.html: Starting gold buys weapons and armour. Both lists are partial — they carry the entries that existed when the system was first drafted, and more will be filled in.

ch-magic.title: Spells and Spellcasting
ch-magic.summary: How spells relate to powers, the properties every spell shares, and the current spell list.
ch-magic.summary_html: How spells relate to powers, the properties every spell shares, and the current spell list.
ch-magic.html: Spells are a special category of power. They use one skill, one power source, and a common framework of properties, and then each spell adds its own effect on top.

ch-overview.title: What Ico Is Trying To Do
ch-overview.summary: The design goals the rules serve, and the single mechanic they all rest on.
ch-overview.summary_html: The design goals the rules serve, and the single mechanic they all rest on.
ch-overview.html:
The Ico adventure system has a short list of goals, roughly in priority order:

  • Fun. It should be fun to play.
  • Storytelling. The rules should push the group towards descriptive

narration of the action rather than away from it.

  • Balance. Two characters built for the same power level should each

feel they contribute equally over a full adventure, and each should have something useful and non-trivial to do in most situations, and especially in combat.

  • Adventure. The standard rules are tuned to make a life of high

adventure less suicidal than the real thing would be: hit points run high relative to weapon damage, skills are impressive, powers are mighty.

  • Simplicity. Not too many dice rolls, not too much arithmetic, not

too many table lookups.

  • Realism. Reality is modelled where doing so does not break one of

the goals above.

ch-powers.title: Powers
ch-powers.summary: The two power sources, how a power is used, and the general powers any character can take.
ch-powers.summary_html: The two power sources, how a power is used, and the general powers any character can take.
ch-powers.html: Powers are the special things a character can do beyond straight skill use — extra attacks, feats of the body, and, as a special case, spells. They draw on one of two internal reserves.

ch-skills.title: Skills
ch-skills.summary: What skills are, how focus tiers cap them, and the full skill list.
ch-skills.summary_html: What skills are, how focus tiers cap them, and the full skill list.
ch-skills.html: Skills are the things a character knows how to do. A higher skill level is greater proficiency. Skills are raised with skill points, which come from character creation and from advancement.

rulebook.title: Ico Adventure System
rulebook.summary: The Ico rules, in reading order.
rulebook.summary_html: The Ico rules, in reading order.
rulebook.html:
Icosahedron: a polyhedron with twenty faces. Almost everything in this game is settled by rolling one twenty-sided die, adding what your character is good at, and seeing whether it was enough.

Read this in order the first time. After that, use the contents above — each rule stands on its own well enough to be looked up in isolation, and the in-game help shows the same text you are reading here.

There are no classes. A character is the sum of the disciplines they have bought into, and a level is simply the next instalment of the budget that buys them.
